'''ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Jurayj al-Rūmī al-Umawī al-Qurashī al-Makkī''' ({{langx|ar|عبد الملك بن عبد العزيز بن جريج الرومي الأموي القرشي المكي}}, 80 AH/699 CE - 150 AH/767 CE) commonly known as Ibn Jurayj ({{IPA|ar|/ʔibn ʒuˈrajʒ/|}}) was an eighth-century [[Tabi'un|''tabi'i'']] ''[[faqīh]]'', exegete and transmitter of [[hadith]]. 

A student of early Meccan jurist [[Ata ibn Abi Rabah]], Ibn Jurayj became a scholar in his own right and served as the [[mufti]] of [[Mecca]] under the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]]. He composed works on [[Tafsir|Quranic exegesis]] and the [[Manasik|rites of pilgrimage]], and his compilation of hadith, ''Kitab al-Sunan'', was a founding work of the [[Musannaf|''musannaf'']] genre. Though lost, much of the latter was preserved in the ''[[Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq|musannaf]]'' of his student [[Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani]], who cites Ibn Jurayj as an informant in approximately one-third of the traditions transmitted. 

==Biography==

=== Early life ===
Ibn Jurayj was born in Mecca in the year 80 AH / 699 CE.<ref name=":2" /> Jurayj is an Arabicized form of the [[Greek language|Greek]] name [[Gregory (given name)|Grēgórios]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |year=2018 |title=Jurayj |encyclopedia=Encyclopaedia of Islam, Three |publisher=Brill |last=Anthony |first=Sean W. |editor1-last=Fleet |editor1-first=Kate |language=en |doi=10.1163/1573-3912_ei3_COM_32885 |editor2-last=Krämer |editor2-first=Gudrun |editor3-last=Matringe |editor3-first=Denis |editor4-last=Nawas |editor4-first=John |editor5-last=Stewart |editor5-first=Devin J.}}</ref> His grandfather Jurayj was of [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] origin and had been a slave owned by Umm Habib bint Jubayr, a [[Mecca|Meccan]] woman from the [[Umayyad dynasty|Umayyad]] clan of [[Quraysh]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |year=2019 |title=Ibn Jurayj |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Canonical Ḥadīth Online |publisher=Brill |language=en |doi=10.1163/2590-3004_ECHO_COM_000073}}</ref> His father  'Abd al-'Azīz was a [[Faqīh|''faqīh'']] and according to a report, was a slave of Fāṭimah bint Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, the daughter of [[Jubayr ibn Muṭʽim|Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim]]. His father was set free, and thus Ibn Jurayj became a client ''(mawlā)'' of the Umayyads, specifically of Umayyah ibn Khālid ibn Asīd. Ibn Jurayj would sometimes affiliate himself with [[Banu Nawfal]] (the family of his mother), and other times with the [[Banu Umayyah]], who were the ''<nowiki/>'iṣbah'' (agnatic kin) of his clientage.<ref name=":04" />{{Reference page|page=15}}<ref name=":3">{{cite book |last=al-Fākihī |first= |author-link=Al-Fakihi |title=Akhbār Makkah fī Qadīm al-Dahr wa-Ḥadīthih |publisher=Dār Khuḍr |year=1994 |editor= |edition=2nd |volume=3 |location=Beirut |page= |language=ar |oclc=187468764}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=187}}

Ibn Jurayj had two ''[[Kunya (Arabic)|kunyas]]'': Abū Khālid and Abū al-Walīd'''.'''<ref name=":032" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=282}} His residence was located on the side of [[Safa and Marwa|Mount Marwa]], and was constructed entirely from white [[gypsum]]; reportedly built by the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyad]] caliph [[Mu'awiya I]] ({{Reign|661|680}}).<ref name=":3" />{{Reference page|page=302}}<ref>{{cite book |last=al-Azraqī |first= |author-link=Al-Azraqi |url=https://shamela.ws/book/9621/620 |title=Akhbār Makkah wa-mā jāʾa fīhā min al-āthār |publisher=Dār al-Andalus |year=1983 |editor= |edition=3rd |volume=2 |location=Beirut, Lebanon |page=237 |language=ar}}</ref>

=== Education ===
At the age of fourteen, he was accepted to the study circle of Meccan jurist [[Ata ibn Abi Rabah|Ata ibn Rabah]] ({{Died in|115/733}}) after previously being rejected twice due to lacking knowledge on [[Quran]] and [[Islamic inheritance jurisprudence|Islamic inheritance laws]] with whom he studied for eighteen to nineteen years.<ref name=":032" />{{Reference page|page=271}}

After Ata's death, he attached himself to his second teacher, [[Amr ibn Dinar]] ({{Died in|126/743-4}}), under whom he studied under for approximately 7 years.<ref name=":032" />{{Reference page|page=271}}<ref>{{cite book |last=al-Fasawī |first= |title=al-Maʿrifah wa-al-Tārīkh |publisher=Dīwān al-Awqāf |year=1974 |edition=1 |volume=2 |location=Baghdad |page=25 |language=ar}}</ref>

=== Travels ===
Ibn Jurayj spent most of his life within the [[Hejaz]], where he may have visited the [[Prophet's Mosque]] in [[Medina]]. He did not travel beyond the region until 143 AH / 760 CE, when, at over sixty-five years of age, he embarked on a journey to [[Yemen]] and subsequently to [[Iraq]].<ref name=":0422">{{cite book |last=Ibn Jurayj |title=Tafsīr al-Qurʾān |publisher=Dār al-Kamāl al-Muttaḥidah |year=2019 |isbn=9789933928216 |editor=ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan Qāniḍ |edition=1st |location=Damascus, Syria |page= |language=ar |chapter=Biography of Ibn Jurayj |oclc=1285066800 |chapter-url=}}</ref>{{Page reference|page=16|pages=}}

He initially travelled to Yemen to meet the governor [[Ma'n ibn Za'ida al-Shaybani]]. According to reports, Ibn Jurayj came to him as a delegate due to a debt he had incurred. He remained with Yemen until the 10th of Dhu al-Qadah. Upon seeing people preparing for Hajj, he requested Ma'n to be sent back to [[Mecca]]. Ma'n hired guides for him, gave him 500 [[Dinar|dinars]], and handed him an additional 1,500. He also gifted him fifteen [[Mule|mules]] loaded with Yemeni goods, bundles of cloth, silver coins, and various types of provisions. He returned to Mecca, arriving just in time for the [[Day of Arafah]].<ref name=":022">{{cite book |last=al-Dhahabī |first=Shams al-Dīn |author-link=Al-Dhahabi |title=Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ |title-link=Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' |publisher=Dār al-Ḥadīth |year=2006 |editor= |volume=6 |location=Cairo |page= |language=ar}}</ref>{{Page reference|page=415}}<ref>{{cite book |last=al-Fākihī |first= |author-link=Al-Fakihi |title=Akhbār Makkah fī Qadīm al-Dahr wa-Ḥadīthih |publisher=Dār Khuḍr |year=1994 |editor= |edition=2nd |volume=2 |location=Beirut |page=384 |language=ar |oclc=187468764}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr |first= |author-link=Ibn 'Abd al-Barr |title=Bahjat al-Majālis wa-Uns al-Majālis |year= |volume=1 |page=808 |pages= |language=ar}}</ref> During his time in Yemen, he was heard by the scholars of [[Sanaa]], including [[Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Ibn Abī Khaythamah |first= |url=https://shamela.ws/book/8477/245 |title=al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr al-Maʿrūf bi-Tārīkh Ibn Abī Khaythamah – al-Safar al-Thālith |publisher=al-Fārūq al-Ḥadīthah li-l-Ṭibāʿah wa-l-Nashr |year=2004 |editor= |edition=1st |volume=1 |location=Cairo |page=330 |language=ar}}</ref>

Ibn Jurayj returned to Mecca, but did not stay long as he was again in debt, eventually pushing him to travel again, this time eastwards to [[Iraq]]. He arrived in [[Basra]] in the latter part of 144 AH / 762 CE and stayed there through 145 AH / 763 CE.<ref name=":022" />{{Page reference|page=409}} The following year, after the construction of [[Baghdad]] was completed in 146 AH / 764 CE by [[Abbasid Caliphate|Abbasid]] caliph [[Al-Mansur|Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr]] ({{Reign|754|775}}), Ibn Jurayj traveled to the city in hopes of receiving a reward.<ref>{{cite book |last=al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī |first= |author-link=Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi |url=https://shamela.ws/book/736/6674 |title=Tārīkh Baghdād |publisher=Dār al-Gharb al-Islāmī |year=2002 |editor= |edition=1st |volume=12 |location=Beirut |page=143 |language=ar}}</ref><ref name=":0422" />{{Page reference|page=|pages=17–18}}

Ibn Jurayj came to al-Mansur, and he still had a debt upon him. He said: "I have compiled the [[Hadith|hadiths]] of your grandfather [[Ibn Abbas]] like no one else has. However, al-Mansur did not give him any reward. Instead, he entrusted him to Sulaymān ibn Mujālid, a man who used to accompany the caliph, and Ḥajjāj ibn Muḥammad al-Muṣayṣī. Sulaymān ibn Mujālid provided him with assistance." So Ibn Jurayj said to him: "I do not know how to repay you, but take my books and have them copied."<ref>{{cite book |last=Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal |first= |author-link=Ahmad ibn Hanbal |url=https://shamela.ws/book/2331/861 |title=al-ʿIlal wa-Maʿrifat al-Rijāl |publisher=Dār al-Khānī |year=2001 |editor= |edition=2nd |volume=2 |location=Riyadh |page=312 |language=ar}}</ref>

Following this, Ibn Jurayj returned to Mecca, where he spent the rest of his years until his death on 11 Dhu al-Hijjah 150 AH / 7 January 768 CE.<ref name=":0422" />{{Page reference|page=19}}

== Views ==
Ibn Jurayj believed in the permissibility of [[Nikah mut'ah|temporary marriage]] (''nikah mut'ah''). The number of ''mut'ah'' marriages he contracted is given variously as 60 by Jarir ibn Abdullah al-Dabbi, 70 by [[Al-Shafi‘i]], and 90 by [[Al-Dhahabi]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Motzki |first=Harald |title=The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence: Meccan Fiqh Before the Classical Schools |publisher=Brill |publication-date=2002 |pages=268–288 |translator-last=Katz |translator-first=Marion H.}}</ref><ref>[[Tadhkirat al-huffaz]] Volume 1 pages 170 -171</ref> although narrations present in later sources describe Ibn Jurayj retracting this opinion.<ref>Talkhis al-Habeer, by [[Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani]], vol 3, page 160, printed in [[Medina]] in 1964.</ref> [[Harald Motzki]] suggests his view on ''mut'ah'' accorded with a Meccan school tradition that was originated by [[Ibn Abbas]] and developed by his student [[Ata ibn Abi Rabah]], and thus did not stem from the [[Sunni Islam|Sunni]]-[[Shia Islam|Shi'ite]] dispute on the matter.<ref name=":0" />
== Works ==
Ibn Jurayj wrote his books on the leaves of ''[[Calotropis procera]]'', and later copied them on parchments. Whenever a hadith scholar would arrive in Mecca, he would show it to him.<ref>{{cite book |author=Sufyān al-Fasawī |title=al-Maʿrifah wa-al-Tārīkh |publisher=al-Irshād Press |year=1974 |editor=Akram Ḍiyāʾ al-ʿUmarī |edition=1 |volume=2 |location=[[Baghdad]] |pages=25–26 |language=ar}}</ref>

=== Kitab al-Sunan ===
Ibn Jurayj compiled a collection of hadith known as ''Kitab al-Sunan'' or ''Al-Jāmiʿ'' (The Comprehensive Collection), which is credited with initiating the ''[[musannaf]]'' genre of hadith literature.<ref name=":04">{{cite book |last=Ibn Jurayj |title=Tafsīr al-Qurʾān |publisher=Dār al-Kamāl al-Muttaḥidah |year=2019 |isbn=9789933928216 |editor=ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan Qāniḍ |edition=1st |location=Damascus, Syria |page= |language=ar |chapter=Biography of Ibn Jurayj |oclc=1285066800 |chapter-url=}}</ref>{{Page reference|page=28|pages=}}<ref name=":032">{{cite book |last=Motzki |first=Harald |author-link=Harald Motzki |title=The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence |date=2021-10-01 |publisher=Brill |isbn=978-90-04-49153-3 |location=Leiden, The Netherlands |pages= |language=en |doi=10.1163/9789004491533}}</ref> His student [[Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani|Abd al-Razzaq]] claimed that he was the first to arrange hadith thematically, arranging them into subject-based chapters.<ref name=":032" /> [[Ibn al-Nadim]] described the work as resembling later ''Sunan'' collections, containing chapters on [[Ghusl|purification]], [[Fasting in Islam|fasting]], [[Prayers in Islam|prayers]], and [[Zakat]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Reinhart |first=A. Kevin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tYyfAwAAQBAJ&dq=ibn+abi+shaybah&pg=PA68 |title=Islamic Law in Theory: Studies on Jurisprudence in Honor of Bernard Weiss |publisher=Brill |year=2014 |isbn=9789004265196 |location=[[Leiden]] |pages=68 |language=en}}</ref> Although the work has been lost, substantial portions are preserved in the [[Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq|''musannaf'' of Abd al-Razzaq]] and other later compilations. Approximately one-third of the traditions found in Abd al-Razzaq's ''Musannaf'' are transmitted from Ibn Jurayj.<ref name=":2">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2016 |title=Ibn Jurayj |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopaedia of Islam|Third Encyclopaedia of Islam]] |publisher=Brill |last=Motzki |first=Harald |author-link=Harald Motzki |editor1=Kate Fleet |language= |doi=10.1163/1573-3912_ei3_COM_30848 |editor2=Gudrun Krämer |editor3=Denis Matringe |editor4=John Nawas |editor5=Everett Rowson}}</ref>

=== Tafsir ===
Ibn Jurayj is credited with composing one of the earliest works of [[Tafsir|Quranic exegesis]] (''tafsir''). More than a dozen students are reported to have studied ''tafsir'' with him, though only five of them are known to have transmitted his ''tafsir'' with certainty. Among them, Ḥajjāj ibn Muḥammad al-Miṣṣīṣī al-A'war ({{Died in|206 AH/820-1 CE}}) transmitted two versions of ''tafsir'' from him: a shorter version that Ibn Jurayj dictated from memory as he did not have the physical copy at that time, and a larger and expansive version that Ibn Jurayj dictated from his written copy. In February 2019, a partial manuscript of the shorter version was identified in the [[Zahiriyya Library]] (formerly catalogued No. 10990), containing commentary on the verses from the middle of [[An-Nisa|Surah Nisa]] to [[Al-Waqi'a|Surah Waqqiyah]].<ref>{{cite book |author=Jurayj |first=Ibn |title=Tafsīr al-Qurān |publisher=Dār al-Kamāl al-Muttaḥidah |year=2019 |isbn=9789933928216 |editor=ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥasan Qāniḍ |edition=1 |location=Damascus, Syria |page=28 |language=ar |chapter=The Transmissions of Ibn Jurayj’s Tafsīr |oclc=1285066800}}</ref>{{Page reference|page=|pages=49–52, 78}}<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1092503725304963075 |user=AQaid |title=مما وفقني الله للكشف عنه وكان منسوبًا لمجهول تفسير الإمام ابن جريج رواية الحسن بن محمد بن الصباح الزعفراني عن الحجاج بن محمد المصيصي عن ابن جريج وهي من أصح روايات تفسيره ولعله أقدم تصنيف يصلنا من وراء القرون |first=د. عبد الرحمن قائد |access-date=24 June 2025 |language=ar}}</ref>

=== Kitāb al-Manāsik ===
Being the [[mufti]] and [[jurist]] of Mecca, he authored a work titled ''Kitāb al-Manāsik'' ('The Book of [[Manasik|Pilgrimage Rites]]'). It contained the knowledge that pilgrims needed annually during the [[Hajj]] season. This may have been an expansion on the chapter of Hajj from his hadith compilation. The transmission of ''Kitāb al-Manāsik'' was extremely rare among later scholars, and the work itself has not survived.<ref name=":04" />{{Page reference|page=29|pages=}}

[[Ahmad ibn Hanbal]] remarked about it: ''"Ibn Jurayj used to narrate to people from other people's books, except during the days of Ḥajj, when he would bring out his own Book of Manāsik and narrate to them from it."''<ref>{{cite book |last=al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī |author-link=Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi |title=al-Kifāyah fī ʿIlm al-Riwāyah |publisher=Dāʾirat al-Maʿārif al-ʿUthmāniyyah |year=1938 |edition=1st |location=Hyderabad, Deccan |page=257 |language=ar |oclc=652204059}}</ref>

== Legacy ==

=== Hadith ===
Hadith transmitted by Ibn Jurayj are present in all six of the [[Kutub al-Sittah|canonical Sunni hadith collections]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ibn Jurayj ابن جريج|url=http://muslimscholars.info/manage.php?submit=scholar&ID=11070|access-date=2020-08-05|website=muslimscholars.info}}</ref> During his stay in Yemen, Ibn Jurayj's lectures were attended by [[ʽAbd al-Razzaq al-Sanʽani]], who included 5,000 of the traditions taught in his ''[[musannaf]]''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Motzki|first=Harald|date=1991|title=The Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Sanʿānī as a Source of Authentic Aḥādīth of the First Century A. H.|url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/545412|journal=Journal of Near Eastern Studies|volume=50|issue=1|pages=1–21|doi=10.1086/373461|jstor=545412|s2cid=162187154|issn=0022-2968|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Ibn Jurayj's status as a hadith transmitter was viewed positively by his student [[Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan]], although he cast doubt on those traditions which had been transmitted from memory and where an informant had been concealed (''tadlis''). The evaluation of Ibn Jurayj being a trustworthy transmitter when not practicing ''tadlis'' was also shared by later hadith critics, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, [[Yaḥya ibn Maʻin|Yahya ibn Maʻin]], and [[Ali ibn al-Madini]].<ref name=":0" /> More recently, Motzki assessed Ibn Jurayj's material in Abd al-Razzaq al-Sanʽani's ''musannaf'', concluding he did not forge the traditions he transmitted.<ref name=":1" /> Due to his tendency to engage in ''tadlis'', medieval hadith scholar [[Muhammad al-Bukhari]] opined that Ibn Jurayj was not a trustworthy transmitter.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Rusdy Qasim, Lc |title=HADIS LEMAH YANG DISEBABKAN OLEH TERPUTUSNYA SANAD (BAGIAN KETIGA) |url=https://markazsunnah.com/3512-2/ |website=markazsunnah |access-date=16 July 2024 |language=Id |year=2021}}</ref>

A student of early Meccan jurist Ata ibn Abi Rabah, Ibn Jurayj became a scholar in his own right and served as the mufti of Mecca under the Umayyads. He composed works on Quranic exegesis and the rites of pilgrimage, and his compilation of hadith, Kitab al-Sunan, was a founding work of the musannaf genre. Though lost, much of the latter was preserved in the musannaf of his student Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani, who cites Ibn Jurayj as an informant in approximately one-third of the traditions transmitted.
